summary: Unequal sharing splits a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable routine: add the ratio numbers to find the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply the value of one part by each person's number of parts to get their share. The core idea children most often get wrong is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = sum of parts), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. A bar/tape diagram cut into (a+b) equal segments makes the equal-parts structure visible and is the canonical representation.
misconceptions: Reading the ratio 2:3 as fractions 2/3 and 3/3 (or 2/3 of the total) instead of 2/5 and 3/5 — using one part as the denominator rather than the sum of parts.
Sharing equally, ignoring the ratio (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each).
Finding the value of one part but forgetting to multiply each share back (reporting the number of parts, or one-part, as the answer).
Unable to combine chained comparisons into a single ratio, so treating 'twice as many' and 'three times as many' as unrelated.

activities.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts
steps: Take a ratio such as 3:5 and draw an empty strip (a tape/bar diagram) to represent the whole quantity.

Decide how many EQUAL segments to cut the strip into so that both children's parts together fill it exactly (try 3, 5 or another number and check), then explain in your own words why the sum 3 + 5 = 8 is the simplest count that works.
Place the total quantity (40) across the strip and work out the value of one segment: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Colour 3 segments for the first child and 5 for the second, then read off 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 5 = 25.
State what fraction of the WHOLE each child gets: 3/8 and 5/8, and check these sum to 1 (and that 15 + 25 = 40).

In a second round, turn chained language ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam, Sam three times as many as Jo') into one ratio Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6 by making the smallest quantity one part, then build that 10-part bar before sharing.
activities.insight: The ratio a:b needs (a+b) equal parts, so each share is a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole — not a/b. One part is the building block; chained comparisons must become a single ratio before sharing.

activities.title: Explain and check the shares
steps: Answer: how many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5, and where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? Say what it would tell you if they did not.

You said the fraction is 3/8 — why is 8 on the bottom and not 5? Test the wrong rule on its own terms: if the 3-part child got 3/5, then by that same rule the 5-part child would get 5/5 (all of them) — do 3/5 and 5/5 fit inside one whole?
Given 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo, 30 altogether', turn it into one ratio (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6) before sharing, and find each share.
activities.insight: Adding the shares back to the original total is a fast self-check, and articulating why the denominator is the sum of parts secures the part-to-whole fraction and the handling of chained comparisons.

activities.title: Short questions to consolidate the routine
steps: Share 40 in the ratio 3:5 and write the two shares.
Choose what fraction of the whole the '3' child gets.
Read a chained-comparison problem and state the combined single ratio before working out the shares.
activities.insight: Separating the share values from the part-to-whole fraction lets the learner spot and discard the 'equal share' and 'a/b of the total' errors.

checkQuestion: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5. Work out how many each child gets. Then tell me: what fraction of ALL the sweets does the child with 3 parts get? Show your working.
checkAnswer: 15 and 25. There are 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, so one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5; the 3-part child gets 3 × 5 = 15 and the 5-part child gets 5 × 5 = 25. The 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.
